newsitem.title: JORDAN: Arab Jordan Investment Bank 1996 pretax profits up.
newsitem.headline: Arab Jordan Investment Bank 1996 pretax profits up.

text.p: Arab Jordan Investment Bank's (AJIB) pre-tax profits rose 5.4 percent to 2.6 million dinars ($3.6 million) in 1996 as investment and commercial business offset a subdued performance by its brokerage arm, the bank said on Wednesday.
"There was growth in commercial business along with improved revenue from investing in international capital markets," Hani al-Qadi, senior deputy general manager, told Reuters.

Pre-tax profits stood at 2.46 million dinars in 1995 and net profits reached 1.92 million dinars in that year. Figures for AJIB's 1996 net profit have yet to be approved by the Central Bank, Qadi said.
AJIB assets grew four percent in 1996 to 224 million dinars from 216.2 million dinars in 1995. Shareholders' equity stood at 25.6 million dinars at end of 1996.
The bank's overall profitabity however was affected by the Amman Financial Market's (AFM) poor 1996 performance and a tight monetary policy that made them pay a higher cost for customer deposits.
"What most directly affected us in 1996 was the sharp decline in volume of trade and prices in the stock market, and high interest rates that squeezed margins," Qadi said.
The bank has a brokerage arm in the AFM whose income along with other brokers was hit by a 40 percent drop in the market's turnover in 1996.
But growing revenues from international market operations and traditional commercial business offset this, Qadi said.

A fast growing international investments division is expected to boost its operations in 1997 helped by new Central Bank's foreign currency liberalisation that allows banks more elbow room to invest in capital markets.
Total loans portfolio rose to 69 million dinars at the end of 1996, from 60.6 million dinars in 1995. AJIB's total deposits grew to 196 million dinars from 145 million dinars in 1995.
AJIB, pending the AGM's approval in April, would double its capital in 1997 to meet a 20 million dinar Central Bank minimum requirement.
Five million dinars will come from reserves under a one-for-two share offer to existing shareholders. Another five million dinars will be raised by a private placement.
The Riyadh-based pan-Arab Investment Company has a 10 percent share in AJIB's 10 million dinar equity. The Libyan Arab Foreign Bank has another 10 percent and Jordan's Housing Bank has 5.7 percent.
Private investors including the Qadi family hold the remaining shares in AJIB, the country's largest of six investment banks.
